Hello,

I maintain **genai_incidents**, an open index of GenAI and agentic-AI security incidents. Our own aggregation is published under CC BY 4.0; each upstream source's terms are recorded and carried through per source. We ingested the AIRI Navigator public bulk-data export while it was available, under AIRI's own **CC BY 4.0** terms — the licence stated at airisk.mit.edu, which AIRI Navigator's own Terms of Use names as the source of the data it presents.

That bulk download is no longer reachable: the ZIP now returns a 404, and the on-page download link appears to have been withdrawn rather than simply moved or broken. When we noticed, we stopped relying on the ingest rather than working around the missing file — we are not scraping the site to reconstruct the dataset by other means.

Two things we'd value your help with:

1. **Is there a sanctioned export or API for this data now, or planned?** We're glad to work within whatever terms you'd prefer — rate limits, an access-request process, a specific attribution format, anything else.

2. **A licensing provenance question**, a more precise version of something we also asked via the AIRI Navigator site on 27 July: part of the AIRI dataset appears to derive from the AI Incident Database, whose incidents collection is licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0 — a share-alike licence, distinct from AIRI Navigator's own CC BY 4.0. Do AIID-derived records within the AIRI dataset carry AIID's share-alike obligation through to downstream users like us, or does AIRI's own CC BY 4.0 grant cover them as redistributed? We're asking about your own understanding of the data's provenance, not raising a concern about your licensing choices — it's the kind of thing that's cheap for you to answer and hard for us to work out independently.

For context on why this matters on our end: roughly 1,380 of the incidents we index carry EU AI Act risk-tier tags derived from AIRI Navigator data, along with AIRI's deployment-stage classification on those same records, its causal-intent classification on about 670 of them, its severity assessment on about 800, and OWASP LLM/ASI risk mappings on comparable numbers, these last derived from AIRI's own risk-subdomain classification. All of it is held at our last successful refresh (31 May) rather than removed, while we wait to hear from you. A sanctioned channel would let us keep it current instead of leaving it as a snapshot.

No urgency beyond wanting to get this right — happy to work with whatever's easiest on your end.

Thank you for your time,
[Maintainer name]
genai_incidents

## Facts verified for this draft (internal — not part of the message)

- **AIRI Navigator's own licence — CC BY 4.0.** Originally recorded per `docs/SOURCE_LICENSES.md` §1.4 (red-reviewer + foreman cross-check, 2026-07-16). **Re-verified live a second time during the bounce review, 2026-07-29** (footer + JSON-LD `publishingPrinciples` at `airisk.mit.edu`, per the foreman's bounce report) — a claim asserted back to its own licensor now rests on a same-week check, not a 13-day-old one.
- **ZIP download dead.** Re-verified fresh 2026-07-29: `https://www.airi-navigator.com/downloads/airi-data.zip` → HTTP 404 (WebFetch). Matches the board's 2026-07-16/18 finding (E6, `docs/SOURCE_LICENSES.md` §1.4). **Correction from bounce #1:** the message no longer says "on both hosts we've checked" — the apex 301s to `www`, so both requests resolve to the same 404; the claim was true but added nothing and invited an easy correction from someone who knows their own redirect config.
- **robots.txt permissive, with `/api/` disallowed.** Re-verified fresh 2026-07-29 — full raw contents: `Allow: /` at root; `Disallow:` `/embed/`, `/admin`, `/login`, `/design-system`, `/api/`. Identical to the board's prior finding. (Not currently referenced in the sent message, kept here for completeness.)
- **Withdrawal characterization — hedged, not asserted.** The message says "appears to have been withdrawn," matching `docs/SOURCE_LICENSES.md` §1.4's own hedge ("the withdrawal looks deliberate... rather than an accidental move of the file") and `mit-airi-courtesy.md`'s sent wording ("appears to be gone... appears gated"). E6 on the board states this more flatly ("deliberately withdrawn") but per this task's brief I did not upgrade the hedged board language into an assertion of MIT's intent in an outward-facing message. Bounce #1 confirmed this was the right call, calling it "correctly weaker than the evidence supports."
- **Ingest dead-since / last-successful-refresh dates.** Per D8 and the WS4-T9 report on the board: dead since 2026-06-07, last successful refresh 2026-05-31. **Corrected from bounce #1:** originally flagged here as "not independently re-derived this session (no shell access)" — the foreman has since confirmed this directly against `ingest/_state/source_health.json` (`last_success: 2026-05-31`, `consecutive_failures: 7`), so both dates now rest on a primary-source read, not only the board's prose record.
- **The tag-family figure — corrected from bounce #1, a defect I own the consequence of, not the input.** The message originally cited "~1,100... regulatory-mapping tags that trace back to AIRI Navigator data." **That number and that population didn't match**: ~1,100 is the WS4-T9/E10 *at-risk-on-retirement* figure — the subset that would *lose* the `eu-ai-act-*` tag if AIRI were retired, because retention at `merge_and_dedupe.py:1432` restores only ~280 AIRI-sole rows. Nothing is being retired here (the very next sentence says so), so a retirement-conditional figure had no referent in this message. **The correct figure for "how much AIRI-derived data do we currently hold" is 1,380** — foreman-verified independently: 1,380 rows carry a tier `eu-ai-act-*` tag, and that set is *exactly* the set of rows citing `airi-navigator.com/incidents/` (symmetric difference zero, net of one bare-tag-only row, `INC-02549`, matching E10's own caveat). The message now cites 1,380, plus AIRI-derived-and-retained families the foreman additionally verified: AIRI's deployment-stage tags (`ai-post-deployment`/`ai-pre-deployment`/`ai-other`) on the same 1,380 rows; AIRI's severity assessment differing from AIID's on 798 rows; and (see the two corrections immediately below) causal-intent and OWASP LLM/ASI mappings. I have no shell access to re-derive any of these myself; they are taken from the foreman's bounce reports, sourced to red-reviewer/foreman verification, the same standing this file already extends to other board-sourced figures (e.g. the WS4-T9 dead-since dates above).
- **Bounce #2 correction — causal-intent was bound to the wrong population, a second instance of the same error class as bounce #1's 1,100/1,380 mix-up.** Bounce #1's fix said "intent classifications on those same records" (i.e., on all 1,380) without stating a count. That structure was itself the defect: `scripts/ingest_airi_navigator.py:126-135` shows `eu_ai_act_risk_level` and `causal_timing` (→ deployment-stage) are **value-preserving** — every AIRI row yields a tag, so binding them to the full 1,380 is correct — but `causal_intent` is a **filter**: `if row.get("causal_intent") == "Intentional"`, so only rows with that exact value retain anything; the other 708 of 1,380 discard it entirely. The true population is **672 of 1,380 (48.7%)**, foreman-verified against the code. The message now says "causal-intent classification on about 670 of them," binding the count to the 1,380 explicitly rather than implying full coverage via sentence structure alone.
- **Bounce #2 correction — the courtesy-note "could not yet state with full confidence" claim was false, disproved by git.** `docs/SOURCE_LICENSES.md` §1.4's CONFIRMED CC BY 4.0 finding was transcribed at commit `74ae6710` on 2026-07-16; `docs/outreach/mit-airi-courtesy.md` was added (status `A`, never renamed since) at commit `fd360421` on 2026-07-18 — **two days later**. The confirmation was already on record when the courtesy note was written; the note simply didn't cite it. The header (line 13) now says the courtesy note "did not state" the point, not that it "could not yet state" it — the former is what the timeline actually shows.
- **Bounce #2 addition, per user ruling — OWASP LLM/ASI mappings disclosed alongside severity, same standard.** The gate flagged that disclosing AIRI-derived severity (798) while omitting OWASP LLM (743) and OWASP ASI (774) — both derived by routing AIRI's own risk-subdomain classification through `SUBDOMAIN_MAP` (`scripts/ingest_airi_navigator.py:114-115`) — was an inconsistent standard, and a comparably-sized family left out would have reopened the same partial-enumeration problem this task exists to close. User ruled: disclose both, same standard as severity. The message describes them as "OWASP LLM/ASI risk mappings on comparable numbers" rather than citing 743/774 individually — both are close enough to the ~800 anchor already in the sentence that a single "comparable numbers" descriptor doesn't overstate or understate either, and it avoids implying they're the same count when they're two distinct (if close) figures.
- **Post-commit-hold correction — the trailing "all derived from AIRI's own risk-subdomain classification" over-bound to the whole enumeration, not just the OWASP clause.** Foreman verified against `scripts/ingest_airi_navigator.py`: the five families each come from a distinct AIRI cell — `subdomain_id` (:115) → OWASP LLM/ASI (and, separately, our internal `attack_vector`); `severity_highest` (:117) → severity; `eu_ai_act_risk_level` (:128) → the EU AI Act tier tags; `causal_intent` (:132) → the intent tag; `causal_timing` (:134) → the deployment-stage tag. A trailing modifier reading as scoped to the full list would have told MIT their risk-subdomain field is the origin of all five, when it's the origin of exactly one (OWASP). Fixed by moving to "these last derived from..." so the attribution binds only to the item immediately before it. **Scope note for whoever edits this sentence next: it is quantifier/modifier-sensitive by construction — every trailing or leading qualifier in this enumeration must be checked against which item(s) it actually reaches, not just whether the underlying fact is true somewhere in the list.** This is the third correction in this file from exactly that failure mode (bounce #1's population mismatch, bounce #2's intent-coverage mismatch, and this one) — treat any future edit to this sentence as high-risk for the same class of error.
- **Deliberately NOT disclosed, to guard against over-correcting into a new completeness problem:** AIRI's own narrative *prose* is not part of what's retained and is not mentioned in the message — descriptions match AIRI's narrative on 0 rows, `affected` traces to AIRI uniquely on 0 rows, and titles match AIRI-only on 1 row (per the foreman's bounce report). The completeness fix here is scoped to the *tag/classification* families actually retained, not an invitation to itemize every field the way the AIAAIC correction (E17) had to.
- **Recipient address.** Confirmed via a `mailto:` link found in a raw WebFetch of `airisk.mit.edu`, 2026-07-29 (presence-finding, see header note on why this is lower-risk than an absence claim). Re-confirmed independently during the bounce review as the sole mailto on the page.
- **Transitive-AIID framing.** Drawn from `docs/SOURCE_LICENSES.md` §1.4's "Relicense-compatible" cell and `docs/audits/WS0-E13-database-right-2026-07-18.md`, which state the open question as: does AIRI's CC BY 4.0 grant extend to AIID-derived fields, or does AIID's CC-BY-SA share-alike apply transitively to them. Phrased in the message as a provenance question about MIT's own understanding of their data, per this task's brief — not a challenge to AIRI's licence and not a request for legal advice. **Tightened from bounce #1:** the AIID clause now says "whose incidents collection is licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0" rather than a blanket "publishes under CC BY-SA 4.0" — AIID's own Terms of Use license named collections specifically and expressly exclude the `reports.text` field (`docs/SOURCE_LICENSES.md` §1.2), so an unqualified claim would overstate AIID's own grant.
- **"Freely-relicensed" removed from the opening line — bounce #1 defect, not an advisory.** The original line described genai_incidents as "an open, freely-relicensed index of AI incidents." Wrong on three counts: `NOTICE-DATA` states upstream terms govern wherever more restrictive; the ATLAS/garak text bodies are Apache-2.0 and expressly not relicensed by LICENSE-DATA; and 1,517 rows ship a row-level CC BY-SA marker. It also inverted what the project's architecture does — D2's facts-plus-link reduction and the row-level marker exist precisely to *avoid* relicensing upstream content — and, worst for this recipient, to a CC BY licensor "relicensed" reads as "we apply our own licence to your content," directly undercutting the sentence that follows it asking whether their content carries strings. Replaced with a scope-accurate, architecture-accurate sentence (also correcting "AI incidents" to the README's actual scope, "GenAI and agentic-AI security incidents"). Per the bounce review: do not over-correct by additionally disclosing the AIAAIC row-level marker to MIT — that's a different rights-holder's business and would clutter this ask.
